**If my spouse starts taking her own reduced Social Security benefit at age 62, (9/2026), can she switch** **to a survivor benefit** **upon my death and still receive 100% of a full spousal survivor benefit? I plan on waiting until age 70 (3/2030) to collect my maximum Social Security benefit.**


**I am worried that claiming her own benefit early may affect her chance of a much higher survivor benefit.** ***– Charles***


Charles, this is a great question because the[Social Security](https://smartasset.com/retirement/social-security-calculator) claiming decision is one of the biggest financial decisions that you and your spouse will make in retirement.


That said, your spouse claiming Social Security at age 62 will not automatically lead to her receiving a reduced survivor benefit. She can absolutely receive a “full” survivor benefit in the future, so long as certain criteria are met.

## How Survivor Benefits Work


One of the most important things to know about survivor benefits is that an individual cannot collect both a[survivor benefit](https://smartasset.com/retirement/things-to-know-about-social-security-survivor-benefits) and a[retirement benefit](https://smartasset.com/retirement/social-security-strategies) based on their own work record. For your wife, she would take the larger of her own benefit or what she is entitled to as a survivor benefit. If she begins collecting her own benefit at 62, I’m going to assume that her survivor benefit will be larger.


As I mentioned earlier, your spouse claiming her own benefit has no impact on any future survivor benefit. However, the key to maximizing survivor benefits is to wait to file a claim until[full retirement age](https://smartasset.com/retirement/full-retirement-age) (FRA). Retirement benefits and survivor benefits actually use different age tables to determine full benefits, but for anyone born in 1962 or later, full retirement age is the same: age 67. That age cohort includes your spouse, as you stated she’s 62 as of September 2026.


Now that I’ve laid out the framework for survivor benefits, here are a couple of different scenarios that could impact you and your spouse. For simplicity, the following examples exclude cost-of-living adjustments unless otherwise noted.


## What Happens if You Die While Delaying Social Security?


Let’s say your full retirement benefit at age 67 is $2,000 per month, but you decide to delay collecting it to allow your benefit to increase. Then, you pass away on your 68th birthday. Your retirement benefit would have grown to $2,160 due to 12 months of earning[delayed retirement credits](https://smartasset.com/retirement/delayed-retirement-credits) .


The Social Security Administration states that if a worker dies after full retirement age without receiving benefits, their survivor benefit will reflect the delayed retirement credits earned up to the date of death.


(If you have similar questions related to Social Security and retirement planning,[connect with a financial advisor](https://smartasset.com/retirement/find-a-financial-planner?utm_source=smartasset&utm_medium=referral&utm_campaign=sma__falc_relevant&utm_content=askanadvisorforfeitsurvivorbenefit) who serves your area and see how they can potentially help.)


So, your wife could ultimately collect $2,160 per month in survivor benefits, but she would need to wait until her full retirement age to claim that amount. Based on the information you provided, her full retirement age for survivor benefits is 67. She could continue to collect her reduced retirement benefit and then switch to survivor benefits when she reaches full retirement age.


Also, keep in mind that your spouse won’t increase her survivor benefit by waiting to claim it past her full retirement age. Using the earlier example, the maximum benefit she would be entitled to is $2,160 per month, before subsequent cost-of-living adjustments. There’s no financial benefit to waiting past her full retirement age to begin collecting her survivor’s benefit.

## What Happens If You Die After Age 70?


Let’s imagine that your full retirement benefit is $2,000 per month and that you’re able to follow your current plan and delay taking Social Security until you turn 70. By that point, your benefit would have grown to $2,480 per month.


Now, let’s say that you live to age 75 and, for this example,[annual cost-of-living adjustments](https://smartasset.com/retirement/cost-of-living-adjustment-cola) have increased your benefit to $2,625 per month. Your spouse would benefit from immediately filing a claim because she’s already attained full retirement age. Then, the Social Security Administration would look at her own benefit and her survivor’s benefit ($2,625) and pay her the larger of the two.


The key point is that she would be entitled to a survivor benefit equal to the amount you were receiving at the time of your passing. It doesn’t reset to your age 70 benefit or the benefit at your full retirement age. By waiting beyond full retirement age to take your own Social Security, you would increase payments for your widow.


(And if you have additional questions about planning for survivor benefits,[speak with a financial advisor](https://smartasset.com/retirement/find-a-financial-planner?utm_source=smartasset&utm_medium=referral&utm_campaign=sma__falc_relevant&utm_content=askanadvisorforfeitsurvivorbenefit) and see how they can potentially help.)


## How Claiming Survivor Benefits Early Reduces Payments


As is the case with your own benefits, a widow(er) can elect to claim survivor benefits before their full retirement age. In fact, a widow(er) can claim benefits as early[as age 60](https://smartasset.com/retirement/social-security-benefits-for-widows) .


Now let’s say that you were to die on your 67th birthday (your full retirement age) with a monthly benefit of $2,000 and that your spouse were to claim her survivor benefit immediately at age 62 and six months. Because she would be claiming 54 months before her full retirement age for survivor benefits, her benefit would be reduced by approximately 18.32%.


(And if you need help calculating your benefit at different ages and modeling how different claiming strategies may impact your long-term financial plan, consider working with a[financial advisor](https://smartasset.com/retirement/find-a-financial-planner?utm_source=smartasset&utm_medium=referral&utm_campaign=sma__falc_relevant&utm_content=askanadvisorforfeitsurvivorbenefit) .)


## Bottom Line


Ultimately, your spouse’s decision to claim her own benefit at 62 won’t lead to an automatic reduction in any survivor benefit. These events are separate from one another. That said, how much your spouse would receive in survivor benefits depends on when you pass away, when you decide to claim your benefit and what age your spouse is when she files a claim for survivor benefit.

- Claiming before full retirement age while earning above Social Security’s annual limit[can cause some benefits to be withheld](https://smartasset.com/retirement/what-income-reduces-social-security-benefits) . A different limit applies during the year you reach full retirement age, and the earnings test ends beginning with the month you reach that age. Social Security later adjusts your benefit to account for months when payments were withheld because of earnings. Estimate how much you’ll actually receive while working before relying on benefits to cover expenses.
